html:
Ibrahim Muteferrika's press was the first press in the Ottoman Empire run by a Muslim to print books in Arabic script, set up in Istanbul in 1727. Muteferrika was a Hungarian-born convert, a diplomat and a scholar.

Jewish, Armenian and Greek printers had worked in the empire since soon after Gutenberg, but books in Ottoman Turkish and Arabic had been copied by hand. Muteferrika won a sultan's decree and a ruling from the chief religious scholar, on the condition that he print no religious texts.

His press turned out a small list of books on history, geography, language and military science, including maps. Print runs were small and sales were slow. The press ran only a few years after his death in 1745, and printing in the Muslim world took off only in the 19th century, with Muhammad Ali's press at Bulaq and the Tanzimat reforms.
sum: Ibrahim Muteferrika's press was the first press in the Ottoman Empire run by a Muslim to print books in Arabic script, set up in Istanbul in 1727. Muteferrika was a Hungarian-born convert, a diplomat and a scholar.
